name: Mirror Room
description: Imagine an n × m grid with some blocked cells. The top left cell in the grid has coordinates (1, 1) and the bottom right cell has coordinates ( n , m ) . There are k blocked cells in the grid and others are empty. You flash a laser beam from the center of an empty cell ( x s , y s ) in one of the diagonal directions (i.e. north-east, north-west, south-east or south-west). If the beam hits a blocked cell or the border of the grid it will reflect. The behavior of the beam reflection in different situations is depicted in the figure below. After a while the beam enters an infinite cycle. Count the number of empty cells that the beam goes through at least once. We consider that the beam goes through cell if it goes through its center.
input_specification: The first line of the input contains three integers n , m and k (1 ≤ n , m ≤ 10 5 , 0 ≤ k ≤ 10 5 ) . Each of the next k lines contains two integers x i and y i (1 ≤ x i ≤ n , 1 ≤ y i ≤ m ) indicating the position of the i -th blocked cell. The last line contains x s , y s (1 ≤ x s ≤ n , 1 ≤ y s ≤ m ) and the flash direction which is equal to " NE ", " NW ", " SE " or " SW ". These strings denote directions ( - 1, 1) , ( - 1,  - 1) , (1, 1) , (1,  - 1) . It's guaranteed that no two blocked cells have the same coordinates.
output_specification: In the only line of the output print the number of empty cells that the beam goes through at least once. Please, do not write the %lld specifier to read or write 64-bit integers in С++. It is preferred to use the cin , cout streams or the %I64d specifier.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 274E — Mirror Room [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
